claim: Each taste modality is generally encoded by a single, molecularly defined, population of sensory cells.
source: Each taste modality is generally encoded by a single, molecularly defined, population of sensory cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of taste coding.

claim: Salt stimulates multiple taste pathways in mammals and insects.
source: However, salt stimulates multiple taste pathways in mammals and insects, suggesting a more complex code for salt taste.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, contrasting with the general principle of single-population encoding.

claim: Four GRN classes are activated by salt in Drosophila.
source: After creating a comprehensive molecular map comprised of five discrete sensory neuron classes across the fly labellum, we find that four are activated by salt
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript showing salt responses across different GRN classes.

claim: Two GRN classes exhibit characteristics of 'low salt' cells.
source: we find that four are activated by salt: two exhibiting characteristics of 'low salt' cells, and two 'high salt' classes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing dose-response characteristics and sodium specificity of Gr64f and IR94e neurons.

claim: Two GRN classes exhibit characteristics of 'high salt' cells.
source: we find that four are activated by salt: two exhibiting characteristics of 'low salt' cells, and two 'high salt' classes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing responses to high salt concentrations in Gr66a and Ppk23glut neurons.

claim: Low salt attraction depends primarily on 'sweet' neurons.
source: Behaviorally, low salt attraction depends primarily on 'sweet' neurons, with additional input from neurons expressing the ionotropic receptor IR94e.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments using Kir2.1 expression in Gr64f neurons.

claim: IR94e neurons provide additional input to low salt attraction.
source: Behaviorally, low salt attraction depends primarily on 'sweet' neurons, with additional input from neurons expressing the ionotropic receptor IR94e.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing reduced low salt attraction when IR94e neurons are silenced with tetanus toxin.

claim: High salt avoidance is mediated by 'bitter' neurons and a population of glutamatergic neurons expressing Ppk23.
source: High salt avoidance is mediated by 'bitter' neurons and a population of glutamatergic neurons expressing Ppk23.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments showing that both Gr66a and Ppk23glut neurons are necessary for high salt avoidance.

claim: The impact of Ppk23glut neurons on salt avoidance depends on prior salt consumption.
source: Interestingly, the impact of these glutamatergic neurons depends on prior salt consumption.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing that silencing Ppk23glut neurons affects high salt avoidance in salt-fed but not salt-deprived flies.

claim: Sodium concentrations below 100 mM tend to be attractive.
source: In general, sodium concentrations below 100 mM tend to be attractive, while any salt present at higher concentrations becomes increasingly aversive (Chandrashekar et al., 2010; Lindemann, 2001; Oka et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Salt present at higher concentrations becomes increasingly aversive.
source: In general, sodium concentrations below 100 mM tend to be attractive, while any salt present at higher concentrations becomes increasingly aversive (Chandrashekar et al., 2010; Lindemann, 2001; Oka et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most taste modalities activate a single, molecularly defined, population of peripheral taste receptor cells.
source: Although there is considerable debate about modes of central taste coding, there is strong evidence that most taste modalities activate a single, molecularly defined, population of peripheral taste receptor cells (Yarmolinsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A dual-pathway model for salt taste has been favored in both mammals and insects.
source: However, research in both mammals and insects has favoured a dual-pathway model for salt taste: a low-threshold sodium-specific population of 'low salt' cells mediates attraction, which is overridden at higher concentrations by ion non-specific 'high salt' cells that drive avoidance (Ishimoto and Tanimura, 2004; Lindemann, 2001; Marella et al., 2006; Oka et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Two distinct aversive taste receptor cell types (bitter and sour) contribute to high salt taste in mammals.
source: Moreover, two distinct aversive taste receptor cell (TRC) types (bitter and sour) contribute to high salt taste in mammals (Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Drosophila labellum contains three types of gustatory sensilla.
source: The Drosophila labellum contains three types of gustatory sensilla, each of which harbors 2–4 gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) (Singh, 1997; Stocker, 1994)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Short (S-type) and long (L-type) sensilla have four molecularly and physiologically distinct GRNs.
source: Short (S-type) and long (L-type) sensilla have four molecularly and physiologically distinct GRNs, while intermediate (I-type) sensilla have only two (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Scott, 2018; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intermediate (I-type) sensilla have only two GRNs.
source: Short (S-type) and long (L-type) sensilla have four molecularly and physiologically distinct GRNs, while intermediate (I-type) sensilla have only two (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Scott, 2018; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Extracellular 'tip-recordings' of different sensilla have identified four GRN types: water (W), sugar (S), low salt (L1), and high salt (L2) cells.
source: Extracellular 'tip-recordings' of different sensilla have identified four GRN types: a water (W) cell that responds to low osmolarity; a sugar (S) cell that responds to sweet compounds; a low salt (L1) cell that is sodium-specific; and a high salt (L2) cell that responds to high ionic concentrations (>250 mM) (Fujishiro et al., 1984; Hiroi et al., 2002; Ishimoto and Tanimura, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: S-type L2 cells respond to bitter compounds in addition to high salt.
source: S- and L-type sensilla are thought to have one of each GRN type, with S-type L2 cells responding to bitter compounds in addition to high salt (Meunier et al., 2003)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: I-type sensilla have an S/L1 hybrid cell that responds to sugars and low salt.
source: I-type sensilla were shown to have an S/L1 hybrid cell that responds to sugars and low salt, and an L2 cell that responds to bitters and high salt (Hiroi et al., 2004)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: I-type sensilla have an L2 cell that responds to bitters and high salt.
source: I-type sensilla were shown to have an S/L1 hybrid cell that responds to sugars and low salt, and an L2 cell that responds to bitters and high salt (Hiroi et al., 2004)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: VGlutMI04979-Gal4 labels a single cell per S-type and L-type sensillum in the labellum.
source: VGlutMI04979-Gal4, which is a gene-trap inserted within a VGlut exon, showed expression in a single cell per S-type and L-type sensillum in the labellum (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VGlut+ cells do not overlap with ChAT expression.
source: These cells do not overlap with those expressing a similar gene trap for choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), supporting the idea that VGlutMI04979-Gal4 labels a bona fide population of glutamatergic GRNs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VGlut is not expressed in water (Ppk28), sweet (Gr64f), or bitter (Gr66a) GRNs.
source: Co-labelling of VGlutMI04979-Gal4 with LexA reporters for known sensory neuron populations revealed that VGlut is not expressed in water (Ppk28), sweet (Gr64f), or bitter (Gr66a) GRNs (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1E-G.

claim: All VGlut+ cells are positive for Ppk23.
source: However, all VGlut+ cells were positive for Ppk23 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Ppk23 GRNs are comprised of two distinct subsets: Ppk23glut and Ppk23chat.
source: Further examination of Ppk23 expression revealed that Ppk23 GRNs are comprised of two distinct subsets: most S-type and all L-type sensilla contain a single GRN that expresses Ppk23 and VGlut; and six S-type sensilla, roughly corresponding to those designated as 'S-a' sensilla (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Weiss et al., 2011), have a second Ppk23 GRN that is positive for Gr66a and ChAT (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I and citations to previous literature.

claim: Most S-type and all L-type sensilla contain a single GRN that expresses Ppk23 and VGlut.
source: Further examination of Ppk23 expression revealed that Ppk23 GRNs are comprised of two distinct subsets: most S-type and all L-type sensilla contain a single GRN that expresses Ppk23 and VGlut; and six S-type sensilla, roughly corresponding to those designated as 'S-a' sensilla (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Weiss et al., 2011), have a second Ppk23 GRN that is positive for Gr66a and ChAT (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Six S-type sensilla have a second Ppk23 GRN that is positive for Gr66a and ChAT.
source: Further examination of Ppk23 expression revealed that Ppk23 GRNs are comprised of two distinct subsets: most S-type and all L-type sensilla contain a single GRN that expresses Ppk23 and VGlut; and six S-type sensilla, roughly corresponding to those designated as 'S-a' sensilla (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015; Weiss et al., 2011), have a second Ppk23 GRN that is positive for Gr66a and ChAT (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: IR76b-Gal4 is expressed in many neurons from all four known classes of labellar GRNs.
source: However, IR76b-Gal4 is expressed in many neurons from all four known classes of labellar GRNs, limiting its utility as a marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: IR94e-Gal4 is expressed in one cell per L-type sensillum.
source: IR94e-Gal4 is expressed in one cell per L-type sensillum, and does not overlap with Ppk28, Gr64f, or Ppk23 (Figure 1L–N).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1L-N.

claim: IR94e-Gal4 does not overlap with Ppk28, Gr64f, or Ppk23.
source: IR94e-Gal4 is expressed in one cell per L-type sensillum, and does not overlap with Ppk28, Gr64f, or Ppk23 (Figure 1L–N).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1L-N.

claim: Ppk28 neurons show dose-dependent inhibition by salt.
source: As previously demonstrated, Ppk28 neurons show dose-dependent inhibition by salt, as with any osmolyte (Cameron et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2C-D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gr64f GRNs show dose-dependent excitation by salt.
source: In contrast, Gr64f and Gr66a both showed dose-dependent excitation by salt, with Gr64f GRNs activated at a lower threshold.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gr66a GRNs show dose-dependent excitation by salt.
source: In contrast, Gr64f and Gr66a both showed dose-dependent excitation by salt, with Gr64f GRNs activated at a lower threshold.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gr64f GRNs are activated at a lower salt threshold than Gr66a GRNs.
source: In contrast, Gr64f and Gr66a both showed dose-dependent excitation by salt, with Gr64f GRNs activated at a lower threshold.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gr64f responses are sodium-specific.
source: Moreover, Gr64f responses were sodium-specific, while Gr66a also responded to potassium chloride (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gr66a GRNs respond to potassium chloride.
source: Moreover, Gr64f responses were sodium-specific, while Gr66a also responded to potassium chloride (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gr64f operates as a 'low salt' cell type.
source: These results are consistent with Gr64f operating as a 'low salt' cell type, and Gr66a acting as a 'high salt' cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing dose-response characteristics and sodium specificity.

claim: Gr66a acts as a 'high salt' cell type.
source: These results are consistent with Gr64f operating as a 'low salt' cell type, and Gr66a acting as a 'high salt' cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing responses to high salt concentrations and ion non-selectivity.

claim: IR94e neurons display weak activation by 50 mM NaCl.
source: IR94e displayed weak activation by 50 mM NaCl, but no responses to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: IR94e neurons show no responses to salt concentrations higher than 50 mM.
source: IR94e displayed weak activation by 50 mM NaCl, but no responses to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: IR94e neurons display sodium-selective tuning.
source: Further testing of different salts at 100 mM revealed sodium-selective tuning, indicating that IR94e labels a second low salt cell type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: IR94e labels a second low salt cell type.
source: Further testing of different salts at 100 mM revealed sodium-selective tuning, indicating that IR94e labels a second low salt cell type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing weak sodium-specific responses at low concentrations.

claim: Ppk23 neurons show very strong dose-dependent salt responses that are ion non-selective.
source: On the other hand, Ppk23 neurons showed very strong dose-dependent salt responses that were ion non-selective.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Ppk23 GRNs show robust activation by 1 M solutions of sodium chloride, potassium chloride, sodium bromide, potassium bromide, cesium chloride, and calcium chloride.
source: In addition to sodium chloride, we observed robust activation by 1 M solutions of potassium chloride, sodium bromide, potassium bromide, cesium chloride, and calcium chloride (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Ppk23 GRNs do not respond to 1 M concentrations of sucrose.
source: As confirmation that the observed activity is salt-evoked and not a response to high osmolality, we found that Ppk23 GRNs do not respond to 1 M concentrations of sucrose (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Labellar Ppk23 GRNs show only very weak activation to a mixture of two male pheromones in female flies.
source: We observed only very weak activation of Ppk23 neurons in female flies to a mixture of two male pheromones, and no significant responses in male flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Labellar Ppk23 GRNs show no significant responses to pheromones in male flies.
source: We observed only very weak activation of Ppk23 neurons in female flies to a mixture of two male pheromones, and no significant responses in male flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: A primary function of labellar Ppk23 GRNs is to mediate a high salt response.
source: Together, these data suggest that a primary function of labellar Ppk23 GRNs is to mediate a high salt response, and position Ppk23 and Gr66a as markers of two high salt GRN classes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong salt responses and weak pheromone responses observed in calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Ppk23 and Gr66a are markers of two high salt GRN classes.
source: Together, these data suggest that a primary function of labellar Ppk23 GRNs is to mediate a high salt response, and position Ppk23 and Gr66a as markers of two high salt GRN classes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing high salt responses in both populations.

claim: Salt stimulation of Ppk23 GRNs results in predominantly lateral activation of Ppk23 projections.
source: While salt stimulation of Ppk23 GRNs resulted in predominantly lateral activation of Ppk23 projections, bitter stimulation activated medial ring-like projections characteristic of Gr66a (Figure 3A)(Kwon et al., 2014; Thorne et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Bitter stimulation of Ppk23 GRNs activates medial ring-like projections characteristic of Gr66a.
source: While salt stimulation of Ppk23 GRNs resulted in predominantly lateral activation of Ppk23 projections, bitter stimulation activated medial ring-like projections characteristic of Gr66a (Figure 3A)(Kwon et al., 2014; Thorne et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous literature.

claim: Ppk23glut and Ppk23chat both respond to salt.
source: This suggests that Ppk23glut and Ppk23chat both respond to salt, but that only Ppk23chat responds to bitter compounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing salt responses in both subpopulations.

claim: Only Ppk23chat responds to bitter compounds.
source: This suggests that Ppk23glut and Ppk23chat both respond to salt, but that only Ppk23chat responds to bitter compounds.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C-D showing bitter responses only in Ppk23chat neurons.

claim: Ppk23chat, but not Ppk23glut, GRNs exhibit bitter responses.
source: As expected, Ppk23chat, but not Ppk23glut, GRNs exhibited bitter responses; however, both subpopulations showed strong dose-dependent excitation by salt (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Both Ppk23glut and Ppk23chat subpopulations show strong dose-dependent excitation by salt.
source: As expected, Ppk23chat, but not Ppk23glut, GRNs exhibited bitter responses; however, both subpopulations showed strong dose-dependent excitation by salt (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: IR76b is absolutely required for salt-evoked activity in Gr64f GRNs.
source: Calcium imaging in IR76b mutants revealed that IR76b is absolutely required for salt-evoked activity in Gr64f GRNs (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The salt responses of Gr66a GRNs are only mildly decreased in IR76b mutants.
source: By contrast, the salt responses of Gr66a GRNs were only mildly decreased in the mutants, showing that these neurons have a mostly IR76b-independent mechanism for detecting high salt.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Gr66a GRNs have a mostly IR76b-independent mechanism for detecting high salt.
source: By contrast, the salt responses of Gr66a GRNs were only mildly decreased in the mutants, showing that these neurons have a mostly IR76b-independent mechanism for detecting high salt.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing only mild reduction in salt responses in IR76b mutants.

claim: Ppk23 salt responses have a strong dependence on IR76b.
source: Ppk23 salt responses had a much stronger dependence on IR76b, with significantly decreased peak values, compared to controls, at all concentrations tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: IR76b mutants exhibit essentially no salt-evoked activity in the Ppk23glut projection region.
source: IR76b mutants exhibited essentially no salt-evoked activity in this target region, suggesting that IR76b is necessary for both the sodium and potassium salt responses of the Ppk23glut population (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: IR76b is necessary for both the sodium and potassium salt responses of the Ppk23glut population.
source: IR76b mutants exhibited essentially no salt-evoked activity in this target region, suggesting that IR76b is necessary for both the sodium and potassium salt responses of the Ppk23glut population (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing loss of salt responses in IR76b mutants.

claim: IR25a mutants have GRN response profiles similar to those of IR76b mutants.
source: We found that IR25a mutants have GRN response profiles similar to those of IR76b mutants, suggesting that perhaps IR25a and IR76b act in a complex to mediate gustatory salt responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in IR25a mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: IR25a and IR76b may act in a complex to mediate gustatory salt responses.
source: We found that IR25a mutants have GRN response profiles similar to those of IR76b mutants, suggesting that perhaps IR25a and IR76b act in a complex to mediate gustatory salt responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculation based on the similar phenotypes observed in IR25a and IR76b mutants.

claim: Mutations in Ppk23 and Ppk29 have no observable effect on the salt-evoked calcium responses of Ppk23 GRNs.
source: However, in contrast to IR76b and IR25a, mutations in Ppk23 and the related ENaC Ppk29 had no observable effect on the salt-evoked calcium responses of Ppk23 GRNs, consistent with previously reported behavioral tests (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B, [Thistle et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Ppk23, Ppk29 mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ppk23 gene marks a salt-responsive GRN population but does not appear to be involved in salt detection.
source: Thus, the Ppk23 gene marks a salt-responsive GRN population but does not appear to be involved in salt detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of Ppk23 mutations on salt-evoked calcium responses.

claim: Control flies are strongly attracted to 50 mM salt mixed with 2 mM sucrose.
source: As previously reported, control flies are strongly attracted to the salt-containing option, while IR76b mutants lose this attraction (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IR76b mutants lose attraction to 50 mM salt mixed with 2 mM sucrose.
source: As previously reported, control flies are strongly attracted to the salt-containing option, while IR76b mutants lose this attraction (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Control flies avoid 250 mM salt mixed with 25 mM sucrose in favor of 5 mM sucrose alone.
source: In this case, control flies avoid 250 mM salt mixed with 25 mM sucrose in favor of plain sucrose at a lower concentration (5 mM).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: IR76b mutants are severely impaired in high salt aversion.
source: Much like their defects in low salt attraction, IR76b mutants are severely impaired in high salt aversion (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ppk23glut and Ppk28 GRNs are dispensable for low salt attraction.
source: As expected, both Ppk23glut and Ppk28 GRNs were dispensable for low salt attraction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gr64f GRN activity is necessary for attraction to 50 mM NaCl.
source: Focusing on the two GRN classes with low salt tuning properties, we found that Gr64f GRN activity is necessary for attraction to 50 mM NaCl, but expression of Kir2.1 in IR94e GRNs had no effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of Kir2.1 in IR94e GRNs has no effect on low salt attraction.
source: Focusing on the two GRN classes with low salt tuning properties, we found that Gr64f GRN activity is necessary for attraction to 50 mM NaCl, but expression of Kir2.1 in IR94e GRNs had no effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Silencing Gr64f and IR94e neurons together results in behavior indistinguishable from Gr64f silencing alone.
source: Further, silencing Gr64f and IR94e neurons together resulted in behavior indistinguishable from Gr64f silencing alone.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of tetanus toxin in IR94e neurons reduces low salt attraction.
source: Puzzled by the apparent lack of a role for IR94e GRNs in salt attraction, we expressed a different effector – tetanus toxin (TNT) – in these neurons without any temporal restriction with Gal80ts, and observed reduced low salt attraction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Attraction to low salt is virtually eliminated when TNT is expressed in both Gr64f and IR94e GRNs.
source: Moreover, attraction was virtually eliminated when TNT was expressed in both Gr64f and IR94e GRNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sweet GRNs mediate the bulk of low salt attraction, with additional input from the IR94e class.
source: Thus, we conclude that sweet GRNs likely mediate the bulk of low salt attraction, with additional input from the IR94e class.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data from silencing experiments.

claim: Gr66a and Ppk23glut GRNs are both necessary for high salt avoidance.
source: We then tested the role of each high salt GRN class in high salt avoidance and found that Gr66a and Ppk23glut GRNs are both necessary for this behavior (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from silencing experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Silencing Ppk23glut GRNs severely impairs the inhibition of PER by high salt in salt-fed flies.
source: Consistent with our binary choice assay, silencing Ppk23glut GRNs severely impaired the inhibition of PER by high salt (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PER data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rescue of IR76b expression in either Gr66a or Ppk23glut GRNs partially restores high salt avoidance to IR76b mutants.
source: Moreover, rescue of IR76b expression in either Gr66a or Ppk23glut GRNs partially restores high salt avoidance to IR76b mutants (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Salt deprivation weakens salt aversion in control flies.
source: We subsequently repeated this experiment with flies deprived of salt for three days and observed the expected weakening of salt aversion in controls (Figure 5D; p<0.0001 compared to Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Silencing Gr66a GRNs further reduces salt avoidance in salt-deprived flies.
source: Strikingly, while silencing Gr66a GRNs further reduced salt avoidance, silencing Ppk23glut GRNs had no effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Silencing Ppk23glut GRNs has no effect on salt avoidance in salt-deprived flies.
source: Strikingly, while silencing Gr66a GRNs further reduced salt avoidance, silencing Ppk23glut GRNs had no effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The aversiveness of Ppk23glut GRN activation is suppressed by salt deprivation.
source: This suggests that the aversiveness of Ppk23glut GRN activation is suppressed by salt deprivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing no effect of Ppk23glut silencing in salt-deprived flies.

claim: Salt deprivation leads to only a very mild and statistically insignificant reduction in Ppk23glut salt responses.
source: We next asked whether the observed behavioral modulation by salt deprivation would be evident in the calcium responses of these neurons; however, salt deprivation led to only a very mild and statistically insignificant reduction in Ppk23glut salt responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Modulation of Ppk23glut behavioral impact is likely to occur downstream of GRN output.
source: Therefore, modulation is likely to occur downstream of GRN output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant changes in calcium responses despite behavioral modulation.

claim: Sip-induced triggering of Gr64f GRN activation makes a tasteless food source attractive compared to the same food without light stimulation.
source: As expected, sip-induced triggering of Gr64f GRN activation makes a tasteless food source attractive compared to the same food without light stimulation, and this effect is independent of salt deprivation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect of Gr64f GRN activation on food preference is independent of salt deprivation.
source: As expected, sip-induced triggering of Gr64f GRN activation makes a tasteless food source attractive compared to the same food without light stimulation, and this effect is independent of salt deprivation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gr66a activation is strongly aversive for both salt fed and salt deprived flies.
source: Similarly, Gr66a activation is strongly aversive for both salt fed and salt deprived flies.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Activation of IR94e neurons does not produce a detectable phenotype in either salt-fed or salt-deprived conditions.
source: Consistent with their lack of a strong phenotype when silenced, activation of IR94e neurons did not produce a detectable phenotype in either condition.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Stimulating Ppk23glut GRNs is aversive, but only when flies have been pre-fed on a salt-containing diet.
source: However, stimulating Ppk23glut GRNs is aversive, but only when flies have been pre-fed on a salt-containing diet (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Salt need modulates salt avoidance downstream of Ppk23glut GRN activation.
source: This supports a model where salt need modulates salt avoidance downstream of Ppk23glut GRN activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic behavioral data showing state-dependent effects of Ppk23glut activation.

claim: Salt taste is encoded by the combined activity of most to all GRN classes.
source: In contrast to other known taste modalities, which typically activate a single, molecularly defined population of sensory neurons, salt taste is encoded by the combined activity of most to all GRN classes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the calcium imaging data showing salt responses across multiple GRN classes.

claim: Gr64f and IR94e display low salt tuning properties and mediate salt attraction.
source: By identifying markers that cumulatively cover virtually every labellar GRN, we find that two cell types – Gr64f and IR94e – display low salt tuning properties and mediate salt attraction.
evidence: This is a summary of calcium imaging and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gr64f neurons have a relatively low threshold for activation and specificity for sodium.
source: Although Gr64f neurons are also activated by higher concentrations of salt, their relatively low threshold for activation and specificity for sodium are consistent with a low salt GRN identity.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data showing dose-response characteristics.

claim: Gr66a and Ppk23glut act as high salt GRNs, responding ion non-selectively to high concentrations of salt and driving avoidance.
source: Two other cell types – Gr66a and Ppk23glut – act as high salt GRNs, responding ion non-selectively to high concentrations of salt and driving avoidance.
evidence: This is a summary of calcium imaging and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The impact of Ppk23glut activation is suppressed upon salt deprivation.
source: Moreover, the impact of Ppk23glut activation is suppressed upon salt deprivation, providing a means to reduce salt avoidance when need is elevated.
evidence: This is based on behavioral and optogenetic data showing state-dependent effects.

claim: Ppk23glut neurons are the only GRN class to express a marker for glutamatergic, rather than cholinergic, neurons.
source: In addition to the modulation of their behavioral impact, Ppk23glut neurons display some notable characteristics, the most conspicuous being they are the only GRN class to express a marker for glutamatergic, rather than cholinergic, neurons.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data showing VGlut expression.

claim: The aversive nature of Ppk23glut output stands in contrast to what one would predict from their projection morphology.
source: Indeed, the aversive nature of Ppk23glut output stands in contrast to what one would predict from their projection morphology, which looks qualitatively similar to known appetitive (Gr64f, Ppk28), rather than aversive (Gr66a) GRNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of projection patterns observed in immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ppk23glut aversiveness may be mediated through inhibition of appetitive taste pathways.
source: It is possible that Ppk23glut aversiveness is mediated through inhibition of appetitive taste pathways, as glutamate can have excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic effects, depending on the receptor present (Liu and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of glutamate signaling and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ppk23 channel is not required for Ppk23glut salt responsiveness.
source: Although Ppk23glut defines a novel high salt cell, it is important to note that the Ppk23 channel is not required for its salt responsiveness.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in Ppk23, Ppk29 mutants showing normal salt responses.

claim: Weak, but significant Ppk23-dependent pheromone responses have been observed in labellar GRNs.
source: Indeed, weak, but significant Ppk23-dependent pheromone responses have been observed in labellar GRNs, although it's unclear whether these were from Ppk23glut or Ppk23chat cells (Thistle et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: IR76b has been shown to be necessary for gustatory responses to low salt, high salt, calcium, acids, amino acids, fatty acids, and polyamines.
source: To date, IR76b has been shown to be necessary for gustatory responses to low salt, high salt, calcium, acids, amino acids, fatty acids, and polyamines (Ahn et al., 2017b; Chen and Amrein, 2017; Hussain et al., 2016b; Lee et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Gr64f salt responses are completely dependent on IR76b.
source: We find that Gr64f salt responses are completely dependent on IR76b, consistent with its proposed role in low salt taste.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants.

claim: Ppk23glut salt responses require IR76b.
source: Ppk23glut salt responses also require IR76b, but those in Gr66a GRNs do not, indicating two different salt transduction mechanisms in these two high salt cells.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants.

claim: Gr66a salt responses do not require IR76b.
source: Ppk23glut salt responses also require IR76b, but those in Gr66a GRNs do not, indicating two different salt transduction mechanisms in these two high salt cells.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in IR76b mutants.

claim: There are two different salt transduction mechanisms in Gr66a and Ppk23glut high salt cells.
source: Ppk23glut salt responses also require IR76b, but those in Gr66a GRNs do not, indicating two different salt transduction mechanisms in these two high salt cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential requirements for IR76b in these two cell types.

claim: IR76b is primarily permeable to sodium when expressed in heterologous cells (PNa: PK = 1: 0.4).
source: This suggests that, although IR76b is primarily permeable to sodium when expressed in heterologous cells (PNa: PK = 1: 0.4), it may function in complexes with other subunits that confer different ion selectivity in different GRN classes (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: IR76b may function in complexes with other subunits that confer different ion selectivity in different GRN classes.
source: This suggests that, although IR76b is primarily permeable to sodium when expressed in heterologous cells (PNa: PK = 1: 0.4), it may function in complexes with other subunits that confer different ion selectivity in different GRN classes (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of non-sodium-specific responses in Ppk23glut neurons despite IR76b dependence.

claim: Ppk23 GRNs were identified as underlying IR76b-dependent calcium taste avoidance.
source: Recently, Ppk23 GRNs were identified as underlying IR76b-dependent calcium taste avoidance (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ppk23 GRNs respond to high concentrations of all salts tested.
source: Indeed, Ppk23 GRNs respond to high concentrations of all salts tested.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data showing responses to multiple salt types.

claim: IR25a is necessary for salt responses in Gr64f and Ppk23glut GRNs.
source: Moreover, we find that IR25a, which was implicated in Ppk23-mediated calcium taste (Lee et al., 2018), is necessary for salt responses in Gr64f and Ppk23glut GRNs, similar to the requirements for IR76b.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in IR25a mutants and a citation to previous literature.

claim: IR76b and IR25a may act in a complex to mediate salt taste.
source: The similar requirements for IR76b and IR25a also suggest that these two receptors may act in a complex to mediate salt taste, which is consistent with previous evidence that IR25a is a broadly expressed coreceptor (Ahn et al., 2017a; Benton et al., 2009; Cameron et al., 2010; Chen and Amrein, 2017; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on similar mutant phenotypes and citations to previous literature showing IR25a acts as a coreceptor.

claim: Changes in gustatory sensitivity based on internal state are a widespread feature of the fly taste system.
source: Changes in gustatory sensitivity based on internal state are a widespread feature of the fly taste system: starvation potentiates sweet GRN sensitivity and suppresses bitter GRN responses; mating increases taste peg GRN sensitivity to polyamines and behavioral sensitivity to low salt in females; and protein deprivation sensitizes taste peg GRNs to yeast and increases behavioral sensitivity to amino acids (Hussain et al., 2016a; Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; LeDue et al., 2016; Steck et al., 2018; Toshima and Tanimura, 2012; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Salt depletion in humans increases salt palatability.
source: Although modulation of salt taste has not been previously examined in flies, salt depletion in humans increases salt palatability (Beauchamp et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The fly taste system encodes salt as a complex mixture of attractive and repulsive sensory responses.
source: Thus, the fly taste system appears to encode salt as a complex mixture of attractive and repulsive sensory responses.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gr64f and Gr66a GRN classes provide a baseline level of attraction or avoidance to salt.
source: Two GRN classes – Gr64f and Gr66a – provide a baseline level of attraction or avoidance, and this response is then adjusted to need via modulation of a third class of salt-responsive GRNs, Ppk23glut.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the behavioral data showing consistent roles of these neurons across feeding states.

claim: Salt response is adjusted to need via modulation of Ppk23glut GRNs.
source: Two GRN classes – Gr64f and Gr66a – provide a baseline level of attraction or avoidance, and this response is then adjusted to need via modulation of a third class of salt-responsive GRNs, Ppk23glut.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the state-dependent behavioral effects of Ppk23glut neurons.

claim: The apparent specificity of labellar Ppk23glut GRNs to salt may provide an important neural substrate for discrimination between salt and other taste modalities.
source: The apparent specificity of labellar Ppk23glut GRNs to salt may also provide an important neural substrate for discrimination between salt and other taste modalities.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed salt-specific responses of Ppk23glut neurons.
